Article Title: Inspiring story on parenthood: “I gave up my childhood to be able to have my children’s childhood” – What Andre Agassi and wife Steffi Graf’s parenting journey teaches about raising a family
Article Text:
Inspiring story on parenthood: “I gave up my childhood to be able to have my children’s childhood” – What Andre Agassi and wife Steffi Graf’s parenting journey teaches about raising a family

What did Andre Agassi mean when he said, “I gave up my childhood to be able to have my children’s childhood”?

How did becoming a father change Agassi’s view of his own childhood?

How did Steffi Graf fit into Agassi’s approach to raising their children?

What does Agassi’s quote tell us about his idea of parenthood?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Andre Agassi’s words, “I gave up my childhood to be able to have my children’s childhood,” offer a deeply personal look at how becoming a parent changed the tennis legend’s view of his own life. Agassi grew up in a world where tennis was not simply a sport but a major part of his everyday life, with intense training and expectations starting at a very young age. Years later, after becoming one of tennis’ biggest stars, he and his wife, fellow tennis legend Steffi Graf, built a family life around their two children, Jaden and Jaz. For Agassi, watching his children grow gave him the chance to experience some of the simple moments of childhood that he felt he had missed himself.The quote is closely connected to Agassi’s own experience growing up. He started playing tennis as a young child and was pushed toward the sport by his father, Mike Agassi. His father had a clear dream for him: he wanted his son to become one of the best tennis players in the world.That dream eventually came true.Agassi went on to become world No. 1 and won eight Grand Slam singles titles during his career. But reaching that level meant spending much of his childhood training, competing and preparing for professional tennis.For a young child, that kind of life can leave little room for ordinary experiences. Instead of having complete freedom to decide how he wanted to spend his time, Agassi’s days were largely connected to tennis.That is where his famous quote becomes especially powerful.When he says he “gave up” his childhood, he is looking back at the years he spent becoming a professional athlete. But he is also talking about what those sacrifices eventually allowed him to do.His success gave him the freedom to step away from tennis and spend more time with his family. It allowed him to be present as his children grew up.In other words, Agassi may have missed parts of his own childhood, but later he had the opportunity to sit beside his children and watch them experience theirs. For him, that became a kind of second chance.Fatherhood gave Agassi a different way of looking at his past. When he watched Jaden and Jaz grow up, he could see the small moments of childhood from a parent’s point of view.He could watch them discover what they liked, make their own choices and develop personalities separate from their famous parents.Those moments were very different from the childhood Agassi had experienced.His early years were strongly connected to the tennis court. His father believed that constant practice and discipline were necessary if Agassi was going to become a champion. That approach helped produce an incredible tennis career, but it also meant that Agassi’s childhood was far from ordinary.As a father, he wanted something different for his children.Instead of seeing childhood as preparation for a future career, Agassi wanted Jaden and Jaz to enjoy the years they were living through.That is one of the most important ideas behind his quote. He was not simply saying that he wanted to give his children more material things or better opportunities. He wanted to give them time.Time to grow.Time to explore.Time to make mistakes.Time to decide what they wanted for themselves.This became especially important because Agassi knew from personal experience how powerful parental expectations can be. He had spent years trying to become the player his father wanted him to be. As a parent, he had the chance to make sure his own children did not feel that same pressure.Steffi Graf’s role in the family’s story is important because she understood Agassi’s world better than almost anyone. Like her husband, Graf was introduced to tennis at a very young age and went on to become one of the greatest players in the history of the sport.Graf won 22 Grand Slam singles titles and spent years at the top of women’s tennis before retiring in 1999. Agassi and Graf later married and raised their two children, Jaden and Jaz.Together, they had something unusual in common: both parents knew exactly what it took to become a tennis champion, but they also knew the pressure that came with that journey.That understanding appears to have influenced the way they raised their children.Despite having two parents who were global tennis stars, Jaden and Jaz were not simply expected to follow the same path.Jaden developed a passion for baseball rather than choosing tennis as his main sport. Jaz has also been able to follow her own interests. Agassi and Graf have supported their children without making their parents’ careers the center of their lives.That is particularly meaningful when viewed alongside Agassi’s quote.The couple had already achieved what many athletes spend their entire lives chasing. They did not need their children to continue that legacy for them.Instead, they could give their children something that both parents understood the value of: choice.Agassi has also spoken warmly about Graf and the role she plays in his life. Their shared experience in professional sports gave them an understanding of the demands and sacrifices that come with elite competition.For their family, giving their children the freedom to choose their own paths became more important than creating another generation of tennis champions.At its heart, Agassi’s quote is about turning his own difficult experiences into something positive for his children.He cannot go back and change the childhood he had. He cannot erase the years of training, pressure and expectations that came with becoming a tennis player.But he can choose what kind of childhood his own children experience.That is what makes the quote about much more than tennis.Many parents work hard because they want their children to have opportunities they did not have themselves. Agassi’s story takes that idea one step further. His goal was not simply to provide his children with a comfortable life. He wanted to be present for the experiences that make childhood special.His words also show that parenthood can change the way people understand their own past.The same childhood that once felt difficult to Agassi became part of what helped him understand his children better. His experiences taught him what pressure can feel like, which may have made him more aware of the importance of giving his own children freedom.And Steffi Graf was there beside him, bringing her own experience as a former champion and a parent.Together, Agassi and Graf chose not to make their children’s lives about living up to their parents’ names. They allowed Jaden and Jaz to build identities of their own.That may be the most powerful part of Agassi’s words.He spent his childhood becoming a tennis champion. But when he became a father, he did not want his children to spend their childhood becoming something for him.He wanted to watch them simply be children.So, when Agassi says, “I gave up my childhood to be able to have my children’s childhood,” he is not only talking about sacrifice. He is talking about perspective, presence and love.He gave years of his life to tennis. Those years helped him become a champion and eventually gave him the freedom to step back and focus on his family.For Agassi, one of the greatest rewards was not another trophy or achievement. It was being able to watch his children grow up on their own terms, with Graf by his side.That is what makes his quote so relatable. Parenthood does not allow us to rewrite our own childhoods, but it can give us the chance to create a different childhood for the next generation.
Article Summary: Tennis legend Andre Agassi said he gave up his childhood to have his children's childhood. Agassi and wife Steffi Graf raised their two children, Jaden and Jaz. For Agassi, watching his children grow gave him the chance to experience some of the simple moments of childhood that he felt he had missed.

Manav Suthar has wasted little time making an impression in Test cricket, with the left-arm spinner already putting himself in the conversation for a bigger role in India’s red-ball plans.Suthar has claimed 23 wickets from his first three Tests, but his impact has gone beyond the numbers. His ability to generate drift, combine it with a deceptive release and consistently hit the right areas has made him an awkward proposition for batters. Ajinkya Rahane has been particularly impressed by the early signs from the youngster. The former India captain believes Suthar’s biggest strength could be his ability to remain effective without relying heavily on assistance from the pitch."I have noticed two things about Manav. The first thing is that for him, the pitch does not matter, whether it turns or not. His speed through the air helps him deceive the batters. It is important and good that you do not depend on the wicket as a spinner. Then you can do well in any condition. The other thing was the way he altered the speed. He has been a quick learner in just three games. He bowled differently to each batter and used the angles well.Yes, it is early, but he has done well," he said in a video on his Hindi YouTube Channel.The 23 wickets in three matches have given Suthar an impressive beginning to his international career, while his adaptability has added another dimension to his prospects.Suthar’s early performances have already established him as India’s lead spinner. Even during the Sri Lanka tour, he was captain Shubman Gill’s first choice whenever the team needed wickets. Since Ravindra Jadeja is gradually becoming more of a batting all-rounder—especially in overseas conditions, Suthar is expected to be India's leading spinner for the near future.His ability to adjust his pace, angles and approach according to the batter has particularly stood out, strengthening the argument that he can be effective across different conditions.Rahane also turned his attention to India’s next Test assignment in New Zealand, where the conditions are expected to be considerably different from those the team experienced in Sri Lanka.The former India batter believes adapting quickly to the conditions will be central to India’s preparations. He also highlighted the value of match practice ahead of a challenging series."The conditions will be totally different in New Zealand. You need to read the wicket and adapt that way. In the last five to six years, we have seen that the team adapts well. I expect them to prepare well. The good thing was that they played a practice match in Sri Lanka. If they get the time for that in New Zealand too, it will be very crucial for mental and physical preparation, even skill-wise," he expressed.For Suthar, however, the immediate task is to build on an encouraging start. Three Tests and 23 wickets have already given him a platform, while his ability to produce results without depending solely on turning pitches could prove valuable as India look to strengthen their spin options for the future.

Article Title: ‘CoE cannot be only for contracted players’: VVS Laxman on building India’s cricket pipeline
Article Text:

How do they get more exposure?

How has the introduction of the U-15 category for women helped in identifying players?

When you switch roles from administrator to mentor coach, does it help that you see these players up close as an administrator?

When you look back at the almost five years of your journey at NCA/CoE, what’s the most satisfying aspect?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Bengaluru: Giving up a lucrative IPL contract and a thriving commentary career, Indian batting great VVS Laxman took the administrative plunge in December 2021. What began at a modest facility inside the M Chinnaswamy Stadium has since evolved into a much larger assignment, with Laxman now at the helm of the BCCI Centre of Excellence, the state-of-the-art facility on the outskirts of the city.The Hyderabadi, whose playing career was defined by wristy elegance and remarkable resilience, is set to complete his tenure later this year.In an exclusive interview with TOI, Laxman reflects on his journey at the CoE, the changing landscape of Indian cricket and the pathways through which the game can transition, evolve and transform.ExcerptsIt has been a very fulfilling journey. When I started in late December 2021, we were working with a relatively small facility, and today we have a much larger and more comprehensive Centre of Excellence. The then BCCI secretary and current ICC chairman, Jay Shah, deserves tremendous credit for having the vision to invest in this facility and create an ecosystem of this scale. I am also grateful to the leadership for giving me the freedom and trust to develop and execute the vision we had for the CoE.For me, the biggest change is not just the infrastructure but also the ecosystem we have built around it, bringing together coaching, sports science, technology and education.This is extremely important to the BCCI. The CoE cannot be only for contracted players. If we want to strengthen Indian cricket, we have to strengthen the pathway beneath the international level as well.We are therefore trying to give domestic and pathway players greater access to quality coaching, sports science, performance analysis and technology. The idea is to identify potential early and give players the right environment to develop. Ultimately, CoE should contribute to the entire Indian cricket ecosystem, not just one particular group of players.It is a very encouraging trend. Players who have played at the first-class or international level have enormous knowledge and experience, and naturally many of them want to give something back to the game. But playing and coaching are two different skill sets. That is why coach education is important. We help them understand communication, planning, leadership and most importantly, how to transfer their experience to another player. More players are now recognising that their impact on the game can continue well beyond their playing careers.It’s not one session; it’s an ongoing mentoring process. Transition from player to coach doesn’t happen overnight. It is really a change in mindset. As a player, your primary responsibility is your own performance. As a coach, your responsibility is to make other people better. Through our coaching courses, we expose former and current players to communication, leadership, planning, managing different personalities and understanding individual players. The biggest learning is that coaching is not about showing people how much you know, but it is about helping the player discover how much they can achieve.The scale of our high performance work has grown significantly. Throughout the year, we run programmes across the pathway for both men and women players from the U-16, U-19, and U-23 age groups, as well as targeted specialist skill camps, including fast and spin bowler camps. We now directly support more than 150 players annually, and the impact is clear in the outcomes we are seeing: improved skill levels, stronger readiness for international cricket, and more players progressing successfully through the pathway into higher levels. Our objective is to create a continuous pathway from age group cricket right through to international level.It has been a very exciting process because women’s cricket in India has grown tremendously. The support ecosystem has to grow at the same pace. We are working on a more structured system around women’s cricket. We are also investing in developing coaches and support staff. Importantly, we don’t want to copy the men’s system. Women’s cricket has its own requirements, and we need to develop expertise around those specific needs.That is one of the most rewarding parts of my role. When you see a young player come into the CoE with potential and then watch him develop not just as a cricketer but also as a person, it gives you enormous satisfaction. With U-19 players, you are dealing with an important stage of their development. You are not just preparing them for the next tournament; you are trying to give them the habits, discipline, resilience, and awareness for a long career. When you subsequently see them progress into India A or senior cricket, it is incredibly satisfying.So with the under-19s or the A-teams, it's about getting better every day as a player in every aspect of their game. So it's not only about skill, but the mental aspect, the physical aspect, and how they can improve, because at the end of the day, any sport you play, any match you play, if you don't have that competitive spirit, then you're not a sports person.So you go out there to perform, you go out there to win the match and win the series, but at the same time, whether it's with under-19s or with the India players, it's also about measuring objectively how you're progressing after every match.It’s satisfying when you see that progress in a player because the whole endeavour is: Can they reach a stage where they can win matches for the senior Indian team in any international fixture and also perform at the highest level?The domestic circuit and structure is so robust, and there are so many matches happening across the different age groups. There's a lot of emphasis on developing the talent in the North-East.So we have camps which are dedicated to the North-East players, men and women from U-19 to senior age group. It’s great to see that every year the quality of those players has definitely gotten better, and the only way it will get better is if they get more exposure.By playing against good teams. You test yourself and gain confidence only when you play against good teams and do well; that's how they get exposure.We started it three years ago. It allows us to strengthen the bench and see players develop. We have players from the first batch who went on to play for India. G Kamalini was in the first batch of the U-15 tournament, and she played for India. So it's great to see not only the boys, but also the girls, benefiting from the various tournaments and camps we run under the BCCI umbrella.Coaching and mentoring come naturally because, as an India player, my interactions with the youngsters were always very seamless and holistic. You share your experiences, help them evolve and develop as cricketers, and maximise their potential.The administration part is obviously a different experience, and luckily again, the structures in the BCCI system made that seamless as well. The best part of this role is getting to see so many players come, perform, get selected, attend the camps, and repeat the process the next year.So it's great to see some of the players who were attending the U-19 camps in 2022 playing for India in 2025-26.The most satisfying thing has been seeing the ecosystem come together. It is not about one facility or one individual. It is about coaches, SSM professionals, performance analysts, grounds staff, administrators and players all working towards the same objective. I am particularly proud that the CoE has evolved into a place where players don’t come only when they are injured. They come to develop their skills, improve physically, learn and become better cricketers.The most fulfilling part of this journey as the CoE head of cricket has been seeing the players' transformation, and we hope they've now achieved their dream and will continue to bring laurels to the country.Ultimately, the real success will be when these systems continue to benefit Indian cricket for many years to come.
Article Summary: VVS Laxman has been at the helm of the BCCI Centre of Excellence since December 2021. The Hyderabadi is set to complete his tenure later this year. He talks about the changing landscape of Indian cricket and the pathways through which the game can transition.

NEW DELHI: Every fast bowler has his own way of showing aggression. Some try to unsettle batters with eye contact, some stay calm, others rely on yorkers, constant appeals or words. India pacer Prasidh Krishna has a different approach - he believes his aggression is best shown through his bowling.Krishna credited disciplined bowling, strong fielding and an attacking mindset for India’s early success against Sri Lanka. The hosts were reduced to 8/2 before bad light ended Day Two of the second Test at the Sinhalese Sports Club Ground on Monday. India had declared on 503/9 after centuries from Devdutt Padikkal and Dhruv Jurel.The bowlers had only a short window to work with, but Krishna made it count, picking up a wicket with just his second delivery of the second over.Krishna said aggression is not necessarily about showing emotion or getting into a verbal battle with the opposition.“Yeah, I would like to say so. I mean, aggression can come out in different ways, and for me it is about what I'm doing when I'm bowling. It's very easy for people to get away or be distracted by what's happening in the pitch.There's too much happening, there's not too much happening, but I think the focus is still to come in and bowl those areas with full effort,” Krishna told the broadcasters before the start of Day 3’s play.Krishna bowled back of a length outside off and found enough movement from the surface to trouble Lahiru Udara. The Sri Lankan opener edged towards gully, where Yashasvi Jaiswal completed an excellent diving catch to dismiss him for one.Krishna said the wicket was a result of both the conditions and Jaiswal’s fielding effort.“Yeah, I think it was, there’s something in the pitch, of course. Maybe stopped a little bit. There was a bit of seam, and I think credit goes to Jaiswal for the catch that he took. It was an exceptional one. We have been putting in some effort on the field in practice, so I think it just paid off,” he mentioned.India had very little time to bowl before bad light stopped play. Manav Suthar then dismissed Prabath Jayasuriya for two with the final delivery of the day, leaving Sri Lanka at 8/2.Krishna stressed that creating chances is only half the job and the fielders also need to complete the opportunity.“100%. I think 50% of the job is bowling the ball there, getting an edge, but 50% is taking it as well, and we have been pretty good at doing that. I think it's also doing the simple things right, which we have been doing well, and that's what shows,” he added.Krishna also spoke about the need to adjust his length according to the pitch. He said the Indian coaching and analysis staff work together to decide the right approach for each surface.“Length is something that keeps changing with pitches that we play on. So we sit with analysts, coaches, and everything and decide on what's the kind of length that we want to be bowling on different surfaces. And yeah, natural length was something that I could say when I was not playing for the country, but when I'm here I need to be bowling every length that the team wants, and I'm trying to do that,” he concluded.
Article Summary: India pacer Prasidh Krishna believes aggression is best shown through his bowling. Krishna picked up a wicket with just his second delivery of the second over. India had declared on 503/9 after centuries from Devdutt Padikkal and Dhruv Jurel. Sri Lanka were reduced to 8/2 before bad light ended Day Two.

Asked point-blank if she'd been scared to try for another baby after her 2018 miscarriage, the mom of four didn't hedge, she confirmed the fear was real, and it stuck around a lot longer than most people would expect.Kelce first went public with the loss last October, during Pregnancy and Infant Loss Awareness Month, explaining that a doctor's visit before the birth of her eldest daughter, Wyatt, confirmed there was no heartbeat.The timing made it worse, the diagnosis fell on her husband Jason's birthday, and she initially couldn't bring herself to break the news to him that day. This week's episode picked up the thread from a different angle: what actually happened once she and Jason decided to try again.According to Kelce, getting pregnant with Wyatt didn't erase the anxiety, it just reshaped it. In early pregnancy, she found herself checking survival odds on a near-weekly basis, and by the later stages of her second trimester, that worry shifted into wondering whether a baby born that day could make it. She's been candid that this obsessive tracking wasn't necessarily a healthy habit, just one that helped her get through it, and one that carried into her later pregnancies too.Kelce didn't have to revisit this topic; she's already raising four young daughters, and the loss happened years ago.But her reasoning for continuing to talk about it is straightforward. She views grief from pregnancy loss as something with no real end date, capable of resurfacing unexpectedly no matter how much time has passed or how many kids follow.It's a theme she's returned to more than once, and each time she's shared it, she's said the response from others tends to be more stories of loss rather than awkward silence.She was careful not to frame the fear as the end of the story, either. Her bottom line was that avoiding the risk entirely would have meant never having Wyatt at all, so for her, moving forward despite the fear was worth it. It's a message that fits her reputation for being unusually direct about hard topics, and one she's now delivered twice, in two different ways, likely for the benefit of anyone quietly sitting with the same fear.

Bringing motorsport to the community

FIA Girls on Track returns

The 2025-26 ABB FIA Formula E World Championship will end in London this weekend, with Rounds 16 and 17 taking place at Excel London on August 15 and 16. While the title battle is expected to be closely fought, sustainability will also be a major focus at the 2026 Hankook London E-Prix. The event is not only about the final two races of the Formula E season. Its sustainability efforts cover energy, waste, food packaging, community projects, education and opportunities for young people.As the championship reaches its season finale, the London E-Prix aims to show how electric racing can combine competition with efforts focused on sustainability and community impact.The London E-Prix will run on 100% certified renewable mains electricity, supported by solar power generated from Excel London’s eco-friendly extension. Track lighting and buffer zones will use dedicated battery storage systems. This will help eliminate the need for continuous generator use. Any remaining emissions will be fully offset.The event will follow a strict zero-waste-to-landfill policy. Non-hazardous waste will be sent for high-rate recycling. Surplus food waste will be composted on-site using commercial wormeries. Used cooking oil will be recycled into biofuel to power plant and machinery.Materials that cannot be recycled will be converted into clean energy.ID@undefinedCaption not available.Food concessions at the 2026 Hankook London E-Prix will use packaging from Notpla, a fellow B Corp-certified brand.The packaging is made from seaweed and natural plant extracts and is home-compostable. It will replace single-use plastics across catering operations and support a circular economy.Mobile provider giffgaff has joined Formula E as the championship's first-ever B Corp partner.The partnership will support the €25,000 Better Futures Fund initiative with Big Issue Recruit. The project will help 20 young Londoners facing employment barriers through one-on-one coaching, barrier-removal grants, refurbished smartphones with data and paid work placements during London E-Prix race week.Formula E and PIF have relaunched the Driving Force platform, which has already engaged more than 94,000 students globally.The platform uses gamified STEM learning based around the next-generation GEN4 car. It also includes trackside workshops during race week and aims to inspire young people to become future leaders in motorsport and sustainability.Formula E's Community Tour will give more than 380 local residents access to the event through two dedicated sessions.The programme brings together more than 15 community, diversity and youth organisations. It includes career-focused sessions for young adults and track tours for local charity beneficiaries, giving underrepresented groups behind-the-scenes access to electric racing.The FIA Girls on Track programme will return to London, with 150 young women aged 12 to 18 taking part.The programme will offer career panels, garage tours, simulator access and discussions on tackling online cyberbullying in sport. It is supported by Hankook, Motorsport UK and Greenpower.Each participant will also receive four race-day tickets, while eight selected participants will take part in the podium ceremony.Also read: 2026 London E-Prix schedule: Round 16 and 17 timings, how to watch Formula E Championship finale and more

Food concessions will use packaging made from seaweed and natural plant extracts. Mobile provider giffgaff has joined Formula E as the championship's first-ever B Corp partner.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Michael J. Fox: "I think the scariest person in the world is the person with…" - a lesson on humour, perspective and facing hard times with lightness
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Michael J. Fox (AP photo)

Quote of the day by Michael J. Fox

"I think the scariest person in the world is the person with no sense of humor"

Where this quote actually comes from

Why humour matters most during genuinely difficult stretches

How humour actually helps people manage stress

Why laughing at your own mistakes actually matters

Why humour can genuinely strengthen relationships

Michael J. Fox's own perspective on adversity

Why humour is not the same thing as avoiding a real problem

Why being naturally serious is not actually a flaw

Other memorable quotes by Michael J. Fox

"One's dignity may be assaulted, vandalized and cruelly mocked, but it can never be taken away unless it is surrendered."

"I am careful not to confuse excellence with perfection."

"Family is not an important thing. It's everything."

"Acceptance doesn't mean resignation; it means understanding that something is what it is and that there's got to be a way through it."

Why people still find meaning in this quote

Humour can genuinely change how a difficult moment actually feels. A stressful situation seems lighter once someone finds a reason to laugh, and a serious problem often becomes easier to approach once it can be seen from another angle. It can create a little distance from fear, frustration and uncertainty, even when the circumstances themselves have not changed. Michael J. Fox , the actor and Parkinson's disease advocate, put a striking twist on that idea. "I think the scariest person in the world is the person with no sense of humor," he said. Not being able to laugh, in his framing, is not simply a personality quirk. It genuinely limits how someone can respond to life, and coming from someone who has lived with a serious, lifelong illness for decades, the line carries a good deal more weight than a passing joke.This line comes from an interview Fox gave to journalist Amy Wallace, published on Reader's Digest's website. Fox is not really suggesting that a humourless person is dangerous in any literal sense. He is pointing at the seriousness that tends to surround someone who cannot laugh at themselves, cannot recognise irony, and cannot find any lightness in a genuinely difficult moment. Humour creates real distance from a problem.It lets someone acknowledge that something is hard without letting it completely take over.Life inevitably brings disappointment, uncertainty and real stress. Humour cannot solve every problem on its own, but it can genuinely change how someone responds to one. Being able to laugh during a hard period offers a small emotional break, and it can help people communicate when a direct, serious conversation feels too uncomfortable to actually have. None of this means every situation deserves to be treated as a joke. Humour and genuine seriousness can exist side by side.Stress tends to narrow someone's attention down entirely onto the immediate problem in front of them. A moment of real laughter can interrupt that cycle. Research into humour and stress has suggested that positive humour can genuinely influence mood and help people cope with stressful experiences, and laughter itself is linked to physiological changes, including a release of muscle tension. None of this should be overstated. Humour is never a substitute for professional help or a practical solution when someone faces a genuinely serious problem. As an everyday coping tool, though, it can offer a genuinely useful shift in perspective.One of the most valuable forms of humour is simply being able to laugh at your own missteps. Nobody gets everything right. People mispronounce words, misjudge situations and occasionally embarrass themselves, and someone who can acknowledge a mistake without being consumed by embarrassment tends to find it easier to actually learn from it. Self-directed humour also tends to make social interactions considerably more comfortable, since it signals that a person does not expect flawless perfection from either themselves or anyone else around them.Shared laughter helps people form real connections. Friends, colleagues and family members often use humour to build a sense of familiarity and trust, and a well-placed joke can break tension that a serious conversation might struggle to shift on its own. There is an important line here worth being clear about, between humour that actually brings people together and humour that humiliates someone else. Jokes built on cruelty or prejudice tend to damage relationships rather than genuinely strengthen them, and the most constructive kind of humour has never really needed anyone else to get hurt.Fox became one of the most recognisable actors of his generation through films and television, including Back to the Future and Family Ties. In 1991, at the age of 29, he was diagnosed with Parkinson's disease. He later made the diagnosis public and became a prominent advocate for Parkinson's research through the Michael J. Fox Foundation. His public approach to living with the condition has consistently included honesty, genuine optimism and humour, which gives his comments about laughter an extra dimension. His point was never that difficult experiences are inherently funny. It is that holding onto a sense of humour can help someone preserve real perspective while actually facing a genuine challenge. His decades-long relationship with humour, cultivated alongside a chronic illness he never chose, reveals that laughter was never a denial of hardship for Fox, but a deliberate, hard-won tool for maintaining perspective and genuine hope through real adversity.There is a meaningful difference between using humour to cope with something difficult and using it to avoid actually dealing with it at all. Some problems genuinely require serious attention and real action, and nobody can simply laugh away financial difficulty, illness or grief. What humour can offer instead is a small amount of emotional breathing space while someone continues addressing the actual underlying issue, which is really the whole distinction worth holding onto here.Fox's quote is deliberately provocative, and it should not be read as suggesting that serious people are inherently unpleasant. Some people naturally have quieter personalities, or simply express humour in a different way. The broader lesson is really about flexibility rather than personality type. Someone who can be genuinely serious when it matters, while still finding moments of humour elsewhere, tends to have more ways of responding to life's challenges than someone who treats every single situation with exactly the same level of weight.Humour is easy to underrate, since it can look insignificant next to more obviously serious qualities like intelligence or discipline. Even so, the ability to laugh genuinely shapes how people communicate, handle their own mistakes and respond to real difficulty. Fox's quote offers a deliberately provocative reminder that life does not always need to be approached with complete seriousness. There will be moments when humour is genuinely inappropriate, and problems that cannot be laughed away at all. In between those moments, though, holding onto a sense of humour tends to keep people connected, flexible and hopeful, which is really the whole point behind the line.
Article Summary: Actor and Parkinson's disease advocate Michael J. Fox gave the quote of the day. He said the scariest person in the world is the person with no sense of humor. Humour can genuinely change how a difficult moment actually feels. A stressful situation seems lighter once someone finds a reason to laugh.

Article Title: Quote of the day by King Charles: "To my darling Mama, as you begin your last great journey to join my dear…" - a tribute to Queen Elizabeth, on gratitude, service and a son's farewell
Article Text:
Quote of the day by King Charles (AP photo)

Quote of the day by King Charles

"To my darling Mama, as you begin your last great journey to join my dear late Papa, I want simply to say this: Thank you. Thank you for your love and devotion to our family and to the family of nations you have served so diligently all these years. May flights of angels sing thee to thy rest"

What is the meaning of King Charles' quote

Why King Charles thanked Queen Elizabeth II

The personal meaning behind "my darling Mama"

What "the family of nations" actually means

Why Charles' farewell centred on service

The Shakespeare reference at the end of the speech

How the quote reflects the relationship between duty and family

How to apply the message in daily life

Some other memorable quotes by King Charles

"I am a dangerous person because I mind about things."

"It is important to be able to stand back and see the bigger picture."

"The environment is something that is very close to my heart."

"I think we have to be very careful about what we do to the natural world."

Few words spoken at a moment of personal loss carry the weight of an entire lifetime. When Queen Elizabeth II died on 8 September 2022, her eldest son, King Charles III, addressed the nation the following day, speaking as both a new monarch and a grieving son at the same time. Recorded in the Blue Drawing Room at Buckingham Palace, with a framed portrait of his mother resting on the desk beside him, his tribute combined personal affection, real gratitude and a recognition of her extraordinary decades of public service. It became one of the most widely remembered moments of that entire period, quoted on front pages across the country the following morning. For millions watching, the address offered a rare glimpse behind the crown, where duty and private grief briefly occupied space. His carefully chosen words also captured the enormous responsibility that had suddenly passed to him, making the moment deeply personal and historically significant.The speech also reassured a grieving public that the values associated with Elizabeth’s reign would continue, while Charles acknowledged the changes that lay ahead. His measured tone reflected both continuity and transition as Britain entered a new chapter.The address also marked the beginning of a new constitutional era, as Charles formally assumed the role his mother had held for seven decades. His message balanced continuity with change, reassuring the public while acknowledging the profound personal loss.At its heart, the message is about gratitude, love and farewell. Charles begins by describing his mother's death as a "last great journey," a gentle way of naming the end of a life, before referring directly to her reunion with her late husband, Prince Philip, who had died in April 2021. Rather than dwelling on the enormous constitutional change actually taking place, Charles places his mother's role firmly within a family context first. He thanks her for the love and devotion she gave to her family, before widening that same gratitude to the people and nations she served. The simplicity of the words "thank you," repeated before he expands on what he is actually grateful for, turns the tribute into an expression of appreciation for an entire lifetime of service.Queen Elizabeth II became monarch in 1952 and remained on the throne for more than seven decades, making her the longest-reigning monarch in British history. Across that period, she served under fifteen British prime ministers and witnessed enormous political, social and technological change. For Charles, though, her significance was never limited to her constitutional role alone. She was also, simply, his mother. His tribute moves between these two identities throughout, recognising her commitment to the "family of nations" she served while speaking about her in the deeply personal language of a son saying goodbye to his parent.The phrase "my darling Mama" gave the speech a genuinely intimate quality that stood apart from the formal language normally associated with royal addresses. Charles was speaking to a global audience, and yet the words themselves were directed towards one single person. Calling his mother "Mama" reflected the private family relationship sitting behind the public institution. Elizabeth II had been Queen to millions of people, but to her son she remained, simply, his mother. That contrast is really what gave the tribute its personal weight rather than letting it feel purely ceremonial.Charles' reference to the "family of nations" reflects Queen Elizabeth II's role across the Commonwealth, a voluntary association of independent countries, many with historical connections to the British Empire, of which she served as Head throughout her entire reign. Her role involved maintaining relationships with leaders and people across every member country, while representing a genuine continuity through decades of political change. Describing these countries as a "family of nations" highlighted exactly the relationships his mother had worked to maintain across the whole of her reign.A central theme running through Queen Elizabeth II's public life was duty. In her 1952 accession broadcast, she pledged her life to the service of the people of the United Kingdom and the Commonwealth. Seven decades later, Charles' farewell returned directly to that same idea. Describing her as having served "so diligently all these years" recognised both the length and the sheer consistency of that commitment. It also reflected the unusual nature of her reign specifically, since she continued carrying out official duties well into her nineties, including appointing Liz Truss as prime minister only two days before her death.Charles closed his tribute with the words "May flights of angels sing thee to thy rest." The line comes from William Shakespeare's Hamlet, Act 5, Scene 2, spoken by Horatio as he mourns his friend at the play's close, "Now cracks a noble heart. Good night, sweet prince, and flights of angels sing thee to thy rest." The reference gave Charles' speech a genuinely literary and solemn conclusion, connecting his personal farewell to one of the most recognisable expressions of grief in English literature, and its suggestion of a peaceful passage into rest made it particularly fitting for a speech delivered the day after losing a parent.One of the most powerful aspects of Charles' tribute is how it brings together two sides of Queen Elizabeth II's life at once, a mother within her own family, and a monarch with responsibilities reaching far beyond it. Charles' words acknowledge both directly, first thanking her for her "love and devotion to our family," then expanding that same gratitude outward to the people and nations she served. In the same speech, he also announced that Prince William and Catherine would become the new Prince and Princess of Wales, and expressed his love for Harry and Meghan "as they continue to build their lives overseas," a reminder that even a historic constitutional address remained, underneath it, a message about family.The circumstances behind this quote are genuinely unique, but its central message of gratitude applies just as well to ordinary relationships. Say thank you while you still can, since the people who matter most should never have to wait for a farewell to hear how much they are actually appreciated. Recognise quiet, unglamorous forms of service, since care and responsibility are often given without much recognition at all. Value family relationships alongside professional achievement, and remember that simple words of love and appreciation tend to become more meaningful, not less, with time.Why King Charles' farewell remains memorableCharles' first address as King carried an unavoidable constitutional significance, and yet its most memorable passage was deeply personal. He was not simply acknowledging the end of a historic reign. He was saying goodbye to the woman who had been his mother for more than seven decades. The repeated "thank you" captures the central emotion of the entire tribute. After a lifetime defined by public duty, Charles chose to close his first address as monarch with something considerably more private, a reminder that behind every title and institution sits an ordinary human relationship. A queen can be a constitutional figure to an entire nation while remaining, simply, "Mama" to her own son.
Article Summary: King Charles III's tribute to Queen Elizabeth II was one of the most widely remembered moments of that entire period. His carefully chosen words captured the enormous responsibility that had suddenly passed to him, making the moment deeply personal and historically significant. His message balanced continuity with change, reassuring the public while acknowledging the profound personal loss.

Article Title: Was Jamal really behind the deletion of IShowSpeed and Kai Cenat’s Minecraft Hardcore world? Viral clip explained
Article Text:
Was Jamal really behind the deletion of IShowSpeed and Kai Cenat’s Minecraft Hardcore world? Viral clip explained

Did Jamal delete IShowSpeed and Kai Cenat’s Minecraft Hardcore world?

IShowSpeed and Kai Cenat’s Minecraft Hardcore run continues

A viral clip from IShowSpeed’s Minecraft Hardcore stream made it look like his brother Jamal had erased the world he and Kai Cenat had spent hours building. That is not what happened. Jamal did delete a saved world while using Speed’s computer, but it was not the active Hardcore world. IShowSpeed later checked the clip himself and confirmed that the world he and Kai were using was still safe.The scare happened after IShowSpeed and Kai Cenat had made their best progress yet in the second edition of their Minecraft Hardcore challenge. On August 11, the pair had full enchanted diamond armor and several Totems of Undying, and they were preparing to face the Warden. They decided to stop for the night after a long session.While Speed was away, Jamal took control of the stream for a short time. He opened the “Select World” menu and clicked on the first saved world, which was named “???.” He then deleted it. Realizing what he had done, Jamal immediately reacted, saying, “Wait! Did I just delete their… No!”That was enough to make the chat fill with “Ls,” as viewers thought the duo had lost their progress.The current save had more than 20 hours of work behind it.Speed later woke up and saw messages telling him Jamal had deleted the world. Once he reached his setup, he watched the clip and checked the name of the active save. His reaction made the situation clear.“He didn’t delete ours. Chat, he didn’t delete ours. Bro, he was close. Nah, ours is [named ‘i got a bad b boat’]… Oh my god, I got scared for a minute.”So, the viral clip shows Jamal deleting a world, but not the one being used for the current Hardcore run. The active save is titled “i got a bad b boat.”The duo’s current challenge is the second edition of their Minecraft Hardcore journey. In their earlier run, they eventually defeated the Ender Dragon after more than 100 hours of gameplay. This time, their goal is bigger, with the Warden, Elder Guardian, Ender Dragon and Wither on their list.As of the latest update, Speed and Kai are on day six of the run and have recorded 42 deaths. Polymarket also listed the death count at 42. IShowSpeed has taken most of those falls. They are now preparing for the Warden, a powerful Minecraft mob with 500 health points, or 250 hearts, and very high attack damage.Their plan is to use their enchanted diamond armor, Iron Golems and Totems of Undying to survive the fight. A Totem can save a player from death when it is held in the correct hand and activated at the right moment.The earlier 2024 run ended with 42 deaths before the pair beat the Ender Dragon, according to Complex. The current challenge is still going, with another major fight ahead for the pair.
Article Summary: IShowSpeed and Kai Cenat had made their best progress yet in their Minecraft Hardcore challenge. Jamal took control of the stream for a short time and deleted a saved world. IShowSpeed later checked the clip himself and confirmed that the world he and Kai were using was still safe.

Article Title: Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu's advice to engineers entering business: Learn to sell, face rejection
Article Text:
As per Sridhar Vembu, selling can also improve communication skills.

Sridhar Vembu says business begins with selling

The simple lesson behind Sridhar Vembu's advice

Moving from engineering, medicine or science into business can require learning a skill that many professionals may not encounter in their regular work: selling. In an X (formerly Twitter) post, Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu shared a simple piece of advice for engineers, scientists and doctors who want to enter the business world—go on sales calls and learn to deal with rejection. Vembu said that technical knowledge alone is not enough to build a business. He argued that speaking directly with potential customers can help professionals explain their ideas better, understand the value of sales and develop the skills needed to run a business.“If you are an engineer or scientist or doctor turning to business, the first thing I would suggest is ‘Please go on a lot of sales calls, face rejection if necessary, but persist’,” Sridhar Vembu wrote in the post.According to Vembu, selling can also improve communication skills. People with technical backgrounds may understand their products or ideas deeply, but explaining them to someone else—and convincing that person to pay for them—is a different challenge.“You will develop better communication skills as you realise that explaining your ideas is not so easy,” he said.Sales calls can also change the way professionals view salespeople.Vembu said people who spend time trying to sell a product may develop greater respect for those whose job involves speaking to customers and handling rejection every day.“You will develop respect for sales people. You may even become good at business!” he added.At the heart of Vembu's post is a basic idea: a business cannot survive without customers and sales.“There is no such thing as a business without selling something. Sometimes the most obvious thing has to be said!” Vembu wrote.
Article Summary: Sridhar Vembu, founder of Zoho, says business begins with selling. Selling can help professionals explain their ideas better, understand the value of sales and develop the skills needed to run a business. Sales calls can also change the way professionals view salespeople.
